House passes its version of the National Defense Authorization Act
US House passes $1.15T defense bill that also deepens Israel ties
sources.text:
The U.S. House narrowly passed a defense policy bill Wednesday authorizing a record $1.15 trillion for the Pentagon.
Though it traditionally sees significant bipartisan support, the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) passed the lower chamber in a 216-212 vote, a sign of the growing polarization under President Donald Trump.
The bill, which must still pass the Senate, provides approximately $250 billion more than the 2026 NDAA, including a 5-7% pay raise for service members.
"This legislation provides our brave servicemembers with an overdue pay raise, strengthens our nuclear deterrence and missile defense – including construction of the Golden Dome," House Speaker Mike Johnson said.
Sponsored by Rep. Mike Rogers, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2027 received support from 209 Republicans, six Democrats and one Independent.
Seven Republicans objected to the bill.
The bill establishes policies and authorities for Department of Defense activities, military construction and Energy Department national security programs.
A major component of the bill, Section 219, establishes the United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative.
The law mandates the Pentagon to designate an executive agent to "expand and accelerate bilateral defense technology research."
The initiative focuses on integrating Israeli-origin and jointly developed technologies into formal U.S. military programs through 2030, covering 10 specific areas including counter-unmanned systems, missile defense and artificial intelligence.
The cooperative efforts also target quantum computing, directed energy and anti-tunneling technology to counter subterranean threats.
The NDAA authorizes the procurement of aircraft and ships while setting active-duty personnel strength levels and military compensation policies.
The bill also addresses Pentagon interactions with partners in Europe and the Asia-Pacific, emphasizing the need for an expedited qualification process for strategic materials such as specified alloys and magnets.
In addition, the legislation mandates that the Defense Department include projected demand for foreign military sales in its munitions production planning.
The bill also sets policy and authorizes appropriations for the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), the Naval Petroleum Reserves and other defense-related programs within the Department of Energy.

sources.news_title: US House passes $1T defense bill despite Iran, Israel concerns
sources.text:
US House passes $1 trillion defence bill despite Iran, Israel concerns
Republicans say the $1 trillion defence bill funds the Iran war, new weapons, troop pay rises and military housing
The US House of Representatives narrowly passed its version of a massive defence policy bill on Wednesday, despite Democrats' concerns about its huge price tag, the Iran war and a provision that would boost Pentagon ties to Israel.
The fiscal 2027 National Defence Authorisation Act, or NDAA, which authorises an unprecedented $1.15 trillion in spending for the military, passed the House by 216 to 212.
The vote was largely along party lines, as all but seven Republicans voted in favour of the measure and all but six Democrats voted against.
Democrats objected to the huge amount of money being authorised for the Pentagon, at a time when President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans are slashing spending on social programs.
They also object to the ongoing and deeply unpopular war with Iran, which the Pentagon said has cost the US $37.5 billion so far.
Republicans said the trillion-dollar spending is essential to support the military as it wages war in Iran, fund defence systems development and equipment purchases and provide benefits for the troops like raises of up to 7% and construction for barracks and family housing.
Another measure that worried Democrats was a provision that would substantially expand military technology cooperation between the United States and Israel, despite calls from many Americans — particularly on the left — to roll back US support for Israel over concern about the heavy toll on Palestinian civilians of its attacks in Gaza.
In 2026, 'must-pass' bill may not pass
Historically seen by both parties as "must-pass legislation", the NDAA is one of the few major bills that always gets through Congress, having become law for 65 straight years.
This year's bill faces major challenges, given deep partisan divisions within Congress on issues ranging from the massive size of the military budget to the Iran war, aid to Israel and Ukraine and "culture war" causes like the treatment of transgender troops.
The fiscal 2027 NDAA's fate was also complicated because Republicans voted to attach it to the "SAVE America Act", Trump-backed legislation to tighten restrictions on voting, before sending it to the Senate. The impact of that decision on the NDAA's fate was unclear, given that there are not enough votes in the Senate to pass the voting law.
Senate Democrats blocked the Senate's version of the NDAA last week. The chamber's Republican leaders have pledged to try again to advance the bill before leaving Washington for their August recess.
It is early in the NDAA process.
Each year, the House and Senate pass their own versions of the NDAA, before Armed Services committee negotiators agree on a compromise version that then comes up for a vote in each chamber.
If the compromise version passes, it would be sent to the White House for Trump to sign into law or veto.

sources.news_title: House Passes Psychedelics Amendments To Codify Trump Executive Order And Extend Military Research Program Until 2033
sources.text:
Politics
House Passes Psychedelics Amendments To Codify Trump Executive Order And Extend Military Research Program Until 2033
The U.S. House of Representatives has voted to extend a psychedelics research effort at the Department of Defense (DOD) for an additional six years and to codify provisions of a psychedelics executive order signed by President Donald Trump earlier this year.
Meanwhile, Republican leadership in the chamber blocked a separate proposal to expand waivers for military recruits who’ve tested positive for marijuana from even being considered.
Lawmakers voted to approve the psychedelics amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2027 in a voice vote on Wednesday as part of an en bloc package with other unrelated proposals, and the overall bill then passed 216-212.
One of the approved measures, sponsored by Reps. Morgan Luttrell (R-TX), Jack Bergman (R-MI), Derrick Van Orden (R-WI), Mike Ezell (R-MS), Troy Carter (D-LA), Morgan McGarvey (D-KY), Lou Correa (DCA), Seth Moulton (D-MA), Sarah Elfreth (D MD) and Michael Rulli (R-OH), seeks to include language in the bill expanding DOD studies on psychedelics that were first authorized under the earlier 2024 NDAA.
That program, signed into law by then-President Joe Biden, directed DOD to establish a process by which active duty service members with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or traumatic brain injury could participate in clinical trials involving psilocybin, MDMA, ibogaine, 5-MeO-DMT and “qualified plant-based alternative therapies.”
As enacted, it only required the secretary of defense to issue updated reports on progress within one year of the law passing and then annually for three years after that. The new amendment would replace “three years” in the law with “nine years.” It also specifies that DOD would have to “extend the performance of research conducted using funding awarded under this section to September 30, 2033.”
The previously enacted legislation, which was also championed by Luttrell, set aside $10 million to fund the military psychedelic studies.
Last month, the House Armed Services Committee approved its version of NDAA and an attached report that calls on military officials to pay greater attention to potential “access pathways” to psychedelic therapies for servicemembers.
Citing a psychedelics executive order signed by President Donald Trump in April, the panel urged DOD leaders to “remain informed of lawful research and access pathways relevant to post-traumatic stress disorder and other serious mental health conditions affecting servicemembers during post-deployment and transition periods, and members of the Reserve Components and National Guard who also serve as first responders.”
That includes studies on “psilocybin-containing investigational products, including naturally derived whole-mushroom formulations administered in structured therapeutic settings,” the report that the panel approved to be attached to NDAA says.
The panel is directing the secretary of defense to issue a report by February 1, 2027 that assesses data on such trials, along with an assessment of “legal and regulatory requirements for expanded access,” including under Trump’s psychedelics executive order as well as a Right to Try law the president signed during his first term in office.
The secretary’s report would also need to include a “proposed timeline for potential pilot activities or expanded clinical research beginning in fiscal year 2027, and for any broader implementation thereafter.”
The second psychedelics amendment approved on the House floor on Wednesday, sponsored by Luttrell, Correa and Rulli, along with Rep. Michael McCaul (R-TX), would codify info federal law parts of the executive order Trump signed in April.
It would require the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to designate an official within 90 days of passage to oversee activities related to “emerging therapeutic interventions” such as ibogaine and other psychedelics, and to coordinate with other federal agencies to do so.
VA would also be directed to submit a report to Congress within 60 days, and then again every two years, on activities related to “emerging therapeutic interventions, including psychedelic-assisted therapies.” It would separately need to work with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to issue a report within 180 days on progress toward implementing Trump’s psychedelics executive order.
The amendment also directs the department to create a workforce implementation-readiness plan for psychedelics and other emerging therapeutic interventions.
“Every day, our nation loses 17 veterans to suicide,” McCaul said ahead of the vote on Wednesday. “These are men and women who survived combat, but then lost to a quiet and longer war against the invisible wounds that they carried with them.”
He spoke about veterans who have had to travel to Mexico to access ibogaine therapy, saying “this needs to be available in the United States of America now in clinical trials for our veterans.”
“Countless vets have told me that they were going to give this one shot before they committed suicide,” he said. “They went down, they experienced ibogaine, and they came back cured.”
Luttrell said in a press release after the vote that “America’s service members and their families deserve nothing less than our full commitment to their readiness, safety, and quality of life.
“This bill delivers on that promise,” he said. “The FY27 NDAA invests in these heroes [and] advances ibogaine and psychedelic-assisted treatment research to battle severe mental health issues… I’m proud of what we secured for our warriors in this year’s bill and look forward to its swift passage in the Senate.”
Meanwhile, lawmakers also used last year’s NDAA to push DOD for a “progress report” on the ongoing psychedelic therapy clinical trials.
Another proposed amendment to the current NDAA from Reps. Dave Joyce (R-OH) and Dina Titus (D-NV), would have expanded waivers for military recruits who’ve tested positive for marijuana—but the House Rules Committee is not allowing it to advance to a floor vote.
The amendment acknowledges that the Army and Navy have already “taken positive steps in their work to design and implement a waiver system that permits potential enlistees into the Armed Forces to reapply for enlistment following a positive toxicology test for tetrahydrocannabinol.”
It calls on the Air Force, Space Force and Marine Corps to follow through, especially “given the ongoing recruitment and retention challenges undermining the Armed Forces readiness goals.”
A similar measure filed by Joyce and Titus, who are co-chairs of the Congressional Cannabis Caucus, was passed by the House of Representatives last year but was not enacted into law.
The current measure would have required those military branches to “develop and implement their own permanent waiver system commensurate with the process employed by the Army and Navy.”
It says that the secretary of defense “shall develop a program through which to provide waivers for potential enlistees into the Armed Forces who were not permitted to enlist following a positive toxicology test for tetrahydrocannabinol so that such potential enlistees are permitted to reapply for enlistment.”
Further, the Department of Defense would have been required to “assess the feasibility of contacting” prospective enlistees who were previously rejected over cannabis and, “to the extent feasible, develop a plan to contact such potential enlistees.”
Within 180 days of enactment, the defense secretary would have needed to submit a report to the congressional committees of jurisdiction with a “plan to create, disseminate, and use a clear definition that highlights that all waivered recruits are qualified and eligible to enlist in the Armed Forces, even if they do not meet every enlistment standard, and that existing standards of enlistment allow for waivers.”
In April, the Army enacted a new policy making it so recruits will no longer need to obtain a waiver to enlist if they have a single conviction for possessing marijuana or drug paraphernalia on their records.

Another drug policy amendment to NDAA that was blocked, from Reps. Madeleine Dean (D-PA) and Nancy Mace (R-SC), would have allowed doctors to administer Schedule I drugs such as certain psychedelics to patients with life-threatening conditions by expanding on the country’s “right to try” law.
The policy creates an exception within the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) that gives qualified patients access to potential therapies that haven’t yet been approved by FDA.
The Dean-Mace proposal is similar to a standalone bill the bipartisan duo filed in Congress late last year.
The lawmakers noted when filing the earlier bill that FDA has designated two psychedelics, MDMA and psilocybin, as breakthrough therapies for the treatment of serious mental health conditions. Yet DEA currently has no pathway to authorize physicians to administer the drugs despite the broader right to try policy, they said.
To address that, the new legislation would amend current statute to allow DEA to register and authorize doctors to administer the novel therapeutics.
In 2024, the House passed a version of NDAA that would have prevented drug testing for marijuana as a condition of enlistment in the military or for commission as an officer. But it was not included in the final version that was signed into law following bicameral negotiations with the Senate.
This month, DOD issued a memo to senior Pentagon leadership making clear that marijuana use by military service members and civilian employees of the department remains prohibited, even as the Trump administration is moving to federally reschedule cannabis.
Lawmakers have also previously considered NDAA amendments to address restrictive military policies prohibiting service members from using hemp products.
In May, the Army published a post reminding soldiers of its “zero-tolerance” policy for all forms of cannabis and its derivatives—including hair care products and lotions made from hemp.
Last year, a memo to Air Force personnel in Massachusetts warned that not only marijuana but also hemp-derived cannabinoids, including CBD and delta-8 THC, are prohibited on military bases and related properties.
In 2022, the Air Force expressed concern that even using CBD-infused hand sanitizer or hemp granola could inadvertently compromise “military readiness.”
DOD more broadly reaffirmed that CBD is off limits to service members in notices published in 2020.
The Navy, for its part, issued an initial notice in 2018 informing ranks that they’re barred from using CBD and hemp products no matter their legality. Then in 2020 it released an update explaining why it enacted the rule change.
The Coast Guard said that sailors can’t use marijuana or visit state-legal dispensaries.
Separately, a general in 2022 said that the Air Force and Space Force were reviewing marijuana policies and considering a “common sense” change that could give potential recruits a pass if they test positive for cannabis.

sources.news_title: Webster backs $1.15 trillion defense bill covering costs of Trump's Iran war - Villages-News.com
sources.text:
U.S. Rep. Daniel Webster voted Wednesday to pass a $1.15 trillion defense policy bill that includes funding to cover the escalating costs of President Donald Trump’s war in Iran.
The fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), or H.R. 8800, passed the House in a narrow 216-212 vote. The result represented a collapse of the normally broad bipartisan coalition that traditionally advances annual national security legislation in Congress. Six Democrats supported the measure, while seven Republicans opposed it.
The legislation advanced with Republicans pushing past Democrats, who argued that Congress is failing to restrain the Trump administration’s expansive use of military force.
Webster, a Republican whose district includes The Villages, praised the bill for focusing on military readiness and supporting troops.
“This legislation fulfills Congress’ constitutional responsibility to provide for our common defense by supporting the men and women who serve our country, and investing in the capabilities needed to deter our adversaries and respond to threats,” Webster said in a statement.
According to the congressman’s office, the defense package includes a 5% to 7% pay raise for service members, fully funds military support for the Department of Homeland Security’s border security mission, and cuts nearly $30 billion by eliminating waste and rolling back diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
The legislation also authorizes nearly $220 billion for next-generation capabilities — such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, hypersonics and space-based technologies — while funding the Golden Dome system, expanding shipbuilding and strengthening nuclear deterrence.

sources.news_title: Aimed at expanding ties with Israel amid Iran war, US House passes historic USD 1.15 trillion defence bill
Sewell rejects GOP defense bill, cites voting provisions and Iran
sources.text:
U.S. Representative Terri Sewell, D-Alabama, voted Wednesday against House Republicans’ fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. Republicans added partisan provisions unrelated to national security, including voting legislation, while dramatically increasing discretionary national security spending to support President Donald Trump’s escalating war with Iran, according to a news release from Sewell’s office.
“One of my most solemn responsibilities as a member of Congress is ensuring that our men and women in uniform have the resources they need to defend our nation,” Sewell said. “That’s why throughout my time in Congress, I have been proud to work across the aisle to craft a strong, bipartisan defense authorization bill.
“Unfortunately, House Republicans have once again abandoned that bipartisan tradition, attaching extreme, partisan provisions that have nothing to do with supporting our troops or strengthening our national security,” Sewell said. “Among them is House Republicans’ voter suppression bill—the SAVE America Act—which has absolutely no place in a bill meant to fund our armed forces. It is extremely troubling that Republicans would attempt to use our annual defense bill to make it harder for eligible Americans, including service members and their families, to exercise their fundamental right to vote.”
Congress has passed the National Defense Authorization Act annually since 1961. The NDAA authorizes funding levels for the Department of Defense and allows the armed forces to pay, train and equip U.S. service members, support America’s allies and conduct essential national security operations.
House Republicans’ fiscal 2027 NDAA includes an unprecedented $1.15 trillion in discretionary defense spending. That figure could reach $1.6 trillion when combined with Republicans’ forthcoming budget reconciliation legislation. The historic price tag comes as the Trump administration seeks additional resources for its escalating military operations in Iran.
“It is unacceptable that Republicans have chosen to bankroll President Trump’s unauthorized and escalating war in Iran, even as American service members continue to lose their lives,” Sewell said. “Congress should be working to bring this conflict to a close—not handing Trump another blank check to put our troops in harm’s way.”
The bill now heads to the U.S. Senate, where it is expected to undergo conference negotiations before returning to both chambers for further consideration.
“I am deeply disappointed that House Republicans have once again chosen partisan politics over our national security,” Sewell said. “I remain hopeful that the Senate will strip these poison pills so that I can once again support a defense authorization bill that puts our troops and our national security first.”

House Passes $1.1 Trillion Defense Bill While Israel Aid Faces Growing Opposition
The House has approved the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), reaffirming US military cooperation with Israel even as support for that relationship faces growing scrutiny on Capitol Hill.
The annual defense policy bill passed 216-212, largely along party lines, with all but seven Republicans voting in favor and all but six Democrats voting against. Alongside a 5% to 7% military pay raise and a provision officially renaming the Department of Defense as “The Department of War,” the legislation commits $750 million to joint US-Israel military programs and launches a new initiative to expand Pentagon technological cooperation with Israel.
The funding package reflects the breadth of the defense partnership. AIPAC said it includes “$500 million for missile defense, $100 million for counter-unmanned systems, $100 million for subterranean operations, and $50 million for emerging technologies. The bill also extends the War Reserves Stockpile Authority–Israel.”

sources.news_title: Trump's Golden Dome, B-21 Bombers, New Submarines and More Win Funding as House Narrowly Approves $1.15 T
sources.text:
The House narrowly passed a nearly $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) in a 216-212 vote, approving billions in funding amid escalating military spending and the war in Iran.
On Wednesday, the funding package was passed for military modernization, weapons programs, pay raises, housing, and President Donald Trump‘s Golden Dome missile defense initiative.
The legislation allocated $56 billion for aircraft programs, including next-generation fighter jets, B-21 Raider bombers, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft, F-35 fighter jets, and Chinook and Black Hawk helicopters. It also authorizes more than $60 billion to build and support a fourth Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine, two Virginia-class submarines, and two Arleigh Burke-class destroyers.
Lawmakers adopted an amendment by Rep. Andy Biggs that would cut the Pentagon’s budget by 0.5% if any part of the Defense Department fails an audit, with the savings directed toward reducing the federal deficit.
The measure was passed by a narrow 216-212 vote, with six Democrats supporting it and seven Republicans opposing it. It now heads to the Senate after being paired with the SAVE Act.
War Funding Plan Draws Criticism
The development comes after the Pentagon raised its estimated cost of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran to $37.5 billion, up from $29 billion in May, as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended a request for nearly $70 billion in supplemental war funding before the Senate.
Hegseth told lawmakers that the funding request is an urgent investment needed to cover operations through September, warning that without it the military would face critical shortfalls.

sources.news_title: Pfluger Secures Big Wins in Defense Bill
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman August Pfluger (TX-11) secured major wins in the FY 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which passed the House. The NDAA is the legislative vehicle that authorizes policies, programs, and spending for the Department of War.
As a U.S. Air Force Academy graduate, fighter pilot with nearly two decades of experience, and retired Colonel in the U.S. Air Force Reserve, Rep. Pfluger has been an outspoken advocate for ensuring this legislation properly equips the Department of War to implement President Trump's National Security agenda of Peace Through Strength. To applaud its passage, Rep. Pfluger released the following statement:
"Today's House passage of the FY2027 NDAA is another decisive step toward President Trump's Peace Through Strength agenda and restoring America's military dominance," he said. "This bill invests in our lethality, arming our forces to deter or defeat any adversary who threatens our nation. It eliminates the waste, fraud, and abuse that has drained resources from our warfighters for years, putting every one of those dollars back into the readiness and capabilities they actually need. Most importantly, it delivers for the men and women who protect our freedom with a pay raise of 5 to 7 percent because service members should never have to worry about providing for their families. This bill reflects our commitment to a stronger, more lethal, and more accountable military."
The bill included several provisions led by Rep. Pfluger to modernize and support our armed forces:
- Pilot Program for Integrated Cognitive Performance for Military Readiness: directs the Secretary of War to establish a pilot program that integrates live performance training, cognitive tools, always-on digital support, and evidence-based sleep and stress resources into a single, integrated capability for our service members and their families. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Reserve Rank Retirement: allows non-regular service to count toward time-in-grade, while explicitly ensuring it cannot be used to calculate retired pay or any other benefit; this is a targeted, fiscally neutral fix that recognizes the value of reserve service. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Service Member Transitional Healthcare Enrollment: addresses the administrative delay that leaves transitioning servicemembers eligible for but unable to enroll in transitional health care for up to 10 days, by requiring the Secretary of Defense to establish a process to enroll members within 2 business days of the start of their eligibility period. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Pilot Program to Evaluate Critical Supply Chain Interference & Infiltration by Adversaries: directs the Secretary of War to stand up a pilot program with private-sector partners to independently and physically verify, at the chipset level, whether commercial electronics used across our military installations are what they claim to be. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Authorized End Strength at the U.S. Air Force Academy: restores the cadet wing to 4,400 cadets and align resources accordingly and commends the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chief of Staff of the Air Force for their attention to this matter, including actions to return USAFA to its statutory capacity. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Strategy to Improve Academic Outcomes at USAFA: requires the Superintendent to submit to the congressional defense committees and the Chairman of the Board of Visitors of the Academy a report containing a strategy to improve academic outcomes at the Academy. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Redesignate the Dean of the Faculty of USAFA as Provost and Dean of the Faculty: redesignates the position of Dean of the Faculty as Provost and Dean of the Faculty. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Review the future of Service Academy Athletics: requires the Secretary of Defense to establish a panel to review the impacts of NCAA rules with respect to compensation of athletes as well as the transfer portal for athletes on the military service academies. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Streamline Congressional Communications with each Board of Visitors: requires the Secretary of Defense to appoint civilian employees for each of the military departments to serve as the congressional communications officials for the Board of Visitors of each of the military service academies. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Revoke Security Clearances for 1260H Lobbyists: requires the Secretary of War to revoke security clearances for former Department of War personnel who engage in lobbying activities on behalf of China. Read the full text of the provision here.
- Pass-Through Budget Transparency: requires the Secretary of War to provide a briefing on the Department’s use, reporting, and management of pass-through funding and efforts to improve transparency in the presentation of such funding within budget justification materials. Read the full text of the provision here.

What is the NDAA and what does the new bill include?
The NDAA is an annual bill that sets defence policy, authorises military programmes and establishes spending limits for the Department of Defense.
Congress has passed an NDAA every year for more than six decades.

The House's top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, Rep. Adam Smith, argued that the bill authorises $1.15 trillion in discretionary spending while pairing it with significant reductions to domestic programmes and tax changes that Democrats oppose.
"I cannot and do not support meeting these needs by making massive cuts to critically important domestic programs and slashing taxes," Smith said.
The final vote reflected those divisions.
Only six Democrats crossed party lines to support the legislation:
- Henry Cuellar (Texas)
- Jared Golden (Maine)
- Vicente Gonzalez (Texas)
- Adam Gray (California)
- Don Davis (North Carolina)
- Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Washington)
Seven Republicans voted against the bill despite backing from House GOP leadership.

The NDAA debate unfolded during escalating US military involvement in the conflict with Iran.

The vote was largely along party lines, as all but seven Republicans voted in favour of the measure and all but six Democrats voted against.
WASHINGTON: The US House of Representatives narrowly passed its version of a massive defence policy Bill on Wednesday (Jul 22), despite Democrats' concerns about its huge price tag, the Iran war and a provision that would boost Pentagon ties to Israel.
The fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA, which authorises an unprecedented US$1.15 trillion in spending for the military, passed the House by 216 to 212.
The vote was largely along party lines, as all but seven Republicans voted in favour of the measure and all but six Democrats voted against.
Democrats objected to the huge amount of money being authorised for the Pentagon, at a time when President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans are slashing spending on social programs.
They also object to the ongoing and deeply unpopular war with Iran, which the Pentagon said has cost US$37.5 billion so far.
Republicans said the trillion-dollar spending is essential to support the military as it wages war in Iran, fund defense systems development and equipment purchases and provide benefits for the troops like raises of up to 7 per cent and construction for barracks and family housing.
Another measure that worried Democrats was a provision that would substantially expand military technology cooperation between the United States and Israel, despite calls from many Americans - particularly on the left - to roll back US support for Israel over concern about the heavy toll on Palestinian civilians of its attacks in Gaza.
IN 2026, "MUST-PASS" BILL MAY NOT PASS
Historically seen by both parties as "must-pass legislation," the NDAA is one of the few major Bills that always gets through Congress, having become law for 65 straight years.
This year's Bill faces major challenges, given deep partisan divisions within Congress on issues ranging from the massive size of the military budget to the Iran war, aid to Israel and Ukraine and "culture war" causes like the treatment of transgender troops.
The fiscal 2027 NDAA's fate was also complicated because Republicans voted to attach it to the "SAVE America Act". Trump-backed legislation to tighten restrictions on voting, before sending it to the Senate. sources.news_title: House Officially Passes Defense Bill with 5% to 7% Military Pay Raise. Here Are 7 More Changes
sources.text:
Military pay raises of up to 7%, faster health care for transitioning service members and several reforms affecting the U.S. Air Force Academy are one step closer to becoming law after the House of Representatives approved its version of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act on Tuesday.
The annual defense policy bill passed the House 216-212, authorizing roughly $1.15 trillion in national security spending while establishing policy priorities for the Department of Defense for the coming fiscal year.
While the legislation still must clear the Senate before reaching President Donald Trump's desk, the House vote provides the clearest picture yet of what lawmakers want to include in next year's defense package.
Here are the seven biggest changes service members and military families should know.
FY2027 NDAA at a Glance
- House vote: Passed 216-212
- Military pay: Proposed raises of 5% to 7%
- Health care: Faster enrollment for transitioning service members
- Reserve retirement: Reserve service could count toward retirement rank
- Air Force Academy: Cadet wing restored to 4,400 and additional reforms proposed
- Supply chain security: New pilot program aimed at protecting military electronics
- Medal of Honor: Legislation advances to recognize Vietnam War hero Maj. Robert Lodge
- Next step: Senate consideration before a final compromise bill
1. Military Pay Could Increase by 5% to 7%
The House bill includes one of the largest proposed military pay raises in years, providing increases ranging from 5% to 7%, depending on rank.
Lawmakers said the increase is intended to improve recruiting and retention while helping military families keep pace with rising costs.
The exact pay raise could still change as the House and Senate negotiate a final version of the bill.
Why it matters: If enacted, the pay raise would directly affect every active-duty service member beginning in fiscal 2027.
2. Transitioning Service Members Could Get Health Care Faster
The legislation would require the Defense Department to create a process allowing eligible service members to enroll in transitional health care within two business days after becoming eligible.
Current administrative delays can leave some troops temporarily unable to enroll despite qualifying for coverage.
Why it matters: Reducing enrollment delays could help eliminate gaps in health care during one of the most significant transitions of a military career.
3. Reserve Service Could Count Toward Retirement Rank
The House bill would allow qualifying non-regular service to count toward time-in-grade requirements for retirement rank.
The proposal specifically states the change would not increase retired pay or other retirement benefits, making it a targeted administrative change rather than an expansion of benefits.
Why it matters: The measure recognizes reserve service while maintaining the current retirement pay structure.
4. The Air Force Academy Could See Several Major Reforms
The legislation includes multiple provisions affecting the U.S. Air Force Academy, including:
- Restoring the cadet wing to its authorized strength of 4,400 cadets.
- Requiring a strategy to improve academic outcomes.
- Renaming the Dean of the Faculty position as Provost and Dean of the Faculty.
- Establishing a panel to study how NCAA athlete compensation and the transfer portal affect the service academies.
- Improving communication between Congress and the Academy's Board of Visitors (USAFA BoV Chairman Rep August Pfluger (TX-11), and Reps Jeff Crank (CO-05), Don Bacon (NE-02), and Don Davis (NC-01)).
Why it matters: Together, the provisions represent one of the most significant collections of Air Force Academy reforms included in recent defense authorization bills.
5. The Pentagon Could Strengthen Supply Chain Security
The House bill directs the Defense Department to establish a pilot program to independently verify commercial electronic components used across military installations.
The goal is to confirm that electronics used by the military are authentic and have not been compromised or infiltrated by foreign adversaries before they enter the supply chain.
Why it matters: As concerns grow over foreign technology and cybersecurity, lawmakers are placing greater emphasis on protecting military systems from compromised components.
6. A Vietnam War Hero Could Finally Receive the Medal of Honor
The legislation authorizes the president to award the Medal of Honor to Maj. Robert Lodge for extraordinary heroism during combat on May 10, 1972, in Vietnam.
If included in the final NDAA and signed into law, the action would recognize Lodge's service more than five decades after the battle.
Why it matters: Congress has increasingly supported reviews of historical valor awards when additional evidence indicates the nation's highest military decoration may be warranted.
7. Cognitive Readiness Could Become a Greater Military Priority
The House bill would establish a pilot program integrating cognitive performance training, sleep resources, stress management tools and digital support into a single capability for service members and their families.
Supporters say the effort recognizes that mental performance, resilience and recovery are critical components of military readiness.
Why it matters: Military leaders have increasingly emphasized that cognitive performance can directly affect operational effectiveness just as physical fitness does.
Other Changes Included in the House Bill
In addition to personnel and readiness initiatives, the House legislation contains several other provisions that are expected to receive significant attention during negotiations with the Senate.
Among them are proposals to rename the Department of Defense as the Department of War, restrict certain TRICARE coverage policies and make other defense policy changes that divided lawmakers during House debate.
Those provisions could be modified or removed as the House and Senate reconcile differences between their respective versions of the NDAA.
What Happens Next
Although House approval is a major step, the NDAA is not yet law.
The Senate is expected to consider its own version of the legislation before negotiators from both chambers meet to resolve differences and produce a final compromise bill.
Only after both the House and Senate pass identical legislation can the measure be sent to President Donald Trump for signature.
Congress has approved a National Defense Authorization Act every year for more than six decades, but significant changes to individual provisions often occur before the final bill reaches the president.
For service members and military families, that means many of the proposals approved by the House, including the military pay raise and quality-of-life initiatives, remain subject to negotiation in the months ahead.

“The Democrats have gone on time and time again with this unprecedented obstruction,” House Budget Committee Chairman Rep. Jodey Arrington, R-Texas, said in the session. “Recently, they blocked the National Defense Authorization Act to protest President Trump and our troops’ efforts to stop this radical terrorist regime from having nuclear weapons,” Arrington said, referring to Senate Democrats blocking that chamber’s version of the 2027 NDAA last week.

“There’s nothing in [the reconciliation bill] whatsoever to bring down costs,” Boyle continued. “Just more spending on the most unpopular war in American history.”
The Iran war has cost the Defense Department $37.5 billion to date, Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators Tuesday. Hegseth testified during a hearing to request $67.1 billion in supplemental money for the war and other DoD expenses.
Historically seen by both parties as “must-pass legislation,” the NDAA is one of the few major bills that always gets through Congress, having become law for 65 straight years.

It authorizes pay raises for troops requested by the Trump administration, including 7% for ranks E-5 and below, 6% for E-6 through O-3 and 5% for ranks O-4 and higher.
The bill includes a proposal to formally rename the Department of Defense to the Department of War after President Donald Trump authorized the use of the name last year. The proposed change is estimated to cost up to $125 million, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
The measure also matches the administration’s requests to grow the force amid a recruiting boon for the services. The Army would add 15,000 soldiers, the Navy 13,000 sailors, the Air Force 8,900 airmen, the Space Force 2,800 guardians and 1,400 Marines.
Democrats took issue with the price tag, and opposed some of the conservative social policy riders, including a ban on gender-affirming care for transgender people.
“This bill advances President Trump’s Peace Through Strength agenda by giving every service member a pay raise, strengthening our defense industrial base, expanding American manufacturing and ensuring our military remains the strongest in the world,” Rep. Steve Scalise, R-La., said in a post on X.
Rep. Adam Smith, of Washington, the ranking Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said the Trump administration’s request is approaching $1.6 trillion if efforts to pay for the war in Iran and increase weapons stockpiles are added.
“The problem is the $1.6 trillion price tag — a 60% increase in the defense budget at a time when our country is running a nearly $2 trillion deficit,” Smith said in a statement. “Our country faces threats, and DOD has modernization needs, but I will not support making massive cuts to critically important domestic programs and slashing taxes to meet those needs.”
The bill will be attached to the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, Trump’s voter ID bill, before being sent to the Senate, which has not yet approved its version of the defense measure. Last week, Senate Democrats blocked its advancement, citing frustration with the Iran war and Trump’s failure to consult with Congress about his decision to send U.S. forces into the conflict.
It’s possible that a final product won’t be ready until after the midterm elections, The Associated Press reported.
Separately, the House adopted a Republican-only $95 billion budget proposal to fund the Iran war and other White House priorities
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators on Tuesday that the cost of the Iran war has risen to $37.5 billion, while stating the Pentagon’s case for supplemental funding, as the conflict stretches into its fifth month.
The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding last month to end the war and enter into a 60-day period of negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program and sanctions relief.
Both nations began trading strikes this month after accusing the other of violating a June ceasefire. Iran has resumed targeting oil tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, and the U.S. Navy reinstated its blockade on Iranian ports.
In total, 18 service members have died and 447 have been injured as part of Operation Epic Fury, according to the Pentagon’s system.

Yasin Gungor and Diyar Guldogan
22 July 2026•Update: 23 July 2026
The US House of Representatives passed a nearly $1.15 trillion annual defense policy bill Wednesday in a narrow 216-212 vote.
Sponsored by Rep. Mike Rogers, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2027 received support from 209 Republicans, six Democrats and one Independent.
Seven Republicans objected to the bill.
The bill establishes policies and authorities for Department of Defense activities, military construction and Energy Department national security programs.
A major component of the bill, Section 219, establishes the United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative.
The law mandates the Pentagon to designate an executive agent to “expand and accelerate bilateral defense technology research.”
The initiative focuses on integrating Israeli-origin and jointly developed technologies into formal US military programs through 2030, covering 10 specific areas including counter-unmanned systems, missile defense and artificial intelligence.
The cooperative efforts also target quantum computing, directed energy and anti-tunneling technology to counter subterranean threats.
The NDAA authorizes the procurement of aircraft and ships while setting active-duty personnel strength levels and military compensation policies. The bill also addresses Pentagon interactions with partners in Europe and the Asia-Pacific, emphasizing the need for an expedited qualification process for strategic materials such as specified alloys and magnets.
In addition, the legislation mandates that the Defense Department include projected demand for foreign military sales in its munitions production planning.
The bill also sets policy and authorizes appropriations for the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), the Naval Petroleum Reserves, and other defense-related programs within the Department of Energy.
Following the voting, House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters that the NDAA will provide a "much-needed" pay raise for US troops and help “rebuild the arsenal of freedom.”
"This was obviously a consequential week for House Republicans, but it was a very consequential week for the American people," Johnson said.
Separately, in a statement, Johnson praised the NDAA, saying the legislation will strengthen the US military, modernize the nation's defenses and advance President Donald Trump's national security priorities.
"The FY27 National Defense Authorization Act will ensure America maintains the most lethal, most dynamic, most capable fighting force in the world," he said.
Johnson also said the bill would reduce defense spending by eliminating $30 billion in "wasteful spending" while strengthening the US defense industrial base.
The legislation stalled in the Senate last week after Democrats blocked the upper chamber's version.
Mounting US troop casualties have complicated efforts to advance the Pentagon's annual policy bill, with public opposition to the Iran war increasing. Since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, a total of 18 American service members have been killed.

They also object to the ongoing and deeply unpopular war with Iran, which the Pentagon said has cost the US $37.5 billion so far.

Historically seen by both parties as “must-pass legislation,” the NDAA is one of the few major bills that always gets through Congress, having become law for 65 straight years.
This year’s bill faces major challenges, given deep partisan divisions within Congress on issues ranging from the massive size of the military budget, to the Iran war, aid to Israel and Ukraine and “culture war” causes like the treatment of transgender troops.

sources.news_title: House Passes $1.15 Trillion Defense Spending Bill
sources.text:
The House passed a more than $1 trillion annual defense bill on Wednesday, moving the unusually contentious measure forward after it earlier stalled in both chambers.
The bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), passed by a 216-212 vote. The House mostly voted along party lines, with Democrats overwhelmingly voting against the measure, citing their objections to President Donald Trump’s war in Iran.
“As we support anything in the defense area, we are de facto supporting this war with no end in sight,” Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said on Wednesday.
The legislation will now need to win approval in the Senate, where it could face a difficult path. Last week, Democrats in the upper chamber blocked the Senate version of the measure for the same reason the majority of their colleagues in the House voted against the bill on Wednesday..
And the House rule that advanced the bill to consideration on the floor of the lower chamber also included language to attach it to a contentious piece of voting legislation before it is sent to the Senate. That measure, the SAVE America Act, would impose stricter ID requirements for voters nationwide, among other provisions. Trump has aggressively pushed for the passage of the SAVE America Act ahead of the pivotal fall midterms, stating that he will not sign any other legislation until it is sent to his desk. House Republicans passed the measure in February, but it has stalled in the Senate, where Republican leaders have said they do not have the votes to pass it.
The NDAA itself would allocate more than $1 trillion to the Department of Defense (DoD), as well as roughly $40 billion to the Department of Energy to oversee the U.S.’s nuclear arsenal and more than $10 billion for other matters related to the military. The package also contains a provision that stipulates that service members will receive a pay raise.
Earlier this year, the President proposed increasing DoD spending to $1.5 trillion—an increase of about $600 billion from last year.
In previous years, Congress has generally approved the annual defense bill with widespread support across the political aisle. But this year, the measure has become snarled in tensions over defense spending levels and the SAVE America Act.
On the House floor on Wednesday, Smith said that many lawmakers are “trying to work in a bipartisan way.”
“But,” Smith continued, “we have to do that against the backdrop of an unbelievably partisan and in many ways out of control Administration and Department of Defense.”
“This year, we have issues that have risen above the normal flow of partisan divide,” he continued, citing the significant proposed increase in the defense budget, as well as the war in Iran.
On June 30, several House Republicans stalled progress on the NDAA and other legislative priorities in an effort to push for stronger action on the SAVE America Act. The standstill stemmed, in part, from the House rule that would have attached the restrictive voter ID legislation with the NDAA after it passed the lower chamber; one GOP lawmaker called the rule a "procedural head fake,” arguing that the Senate could detach the SAVE America Act from the defense bill. The bloc of House Republicans who rebelled against the move called on the party to take more radical steps to pass Trump’s restrictive voter ID law.
Senate Democrats, meanwhile, expressed their frustrations with the ongoing war in the Middle East by preventing the NDAA from moving forward.
On July 14, the measure failed to advance in the upper chamber in a vote of 50-46—a result that fell short of the 60-vote threshold required for it to proceed to the Senate floor. Lawmakers voted largely along party lines.
“The NDAA cannot become a permission slip for that recklessness that we see occurring in Iran,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said before casting his vote. “Donald Trump does not get to drag the American people deeper into a war he cannot explain and does not know how to end—and then demand that Congress look the other way.”
Democrats have repeatedly pushed for greater congressional oversight over the war, which started when the U.S. and Israel launched military strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, is now in its fifth month and has led to the deaths of 17 American service members. The U.S. and Iran agreed to a memorandum of understanding in June that provided the framework for negotiating a final peace deal. But amid conflict over the key Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. resumed strikes against Iran earlier this month, with Trump declaring the tenuous cease-fire under the memorandum “over.”
Several Democrats on the House floor on Wednesday also criticized the increase in defense spending at a time when the Trump Administration has made significant cuts to many health care and social programs. But Republicans argued that the increase is necessary.
“For the first time in 40 years, we’ve been presented a budget that accounts for the true cost of American deterrence,” Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, said on the House floor. “This top line begins to reverse the damage caused by decades of underinvestment in the U.S. military.”
Also on Wednesday, the House adopted a $95 billion budget proposal focused on a number of Trump’s policy priorities, including the war in Iran—a measure that was supported only by Republicans, while Democrats, and two GOP members breaking from the rest of their party, objected to it.

The panel’s top Republican, Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama, has argued the bill is necessary to support troops, foster innovation and strengthen an eroding defense industrial base in the face of China’s growing might.

According to Politico, the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) was approved in a 216-212 vote, with only six Democrats supporting the legislation. Their votes helped Republicans overcome opposition from seven members of their own party.
The passage of the bill marked a victory for Trump and US House Speaker Mike Johnson, who managed to steer the legislation through despite divisions within the Republican ranks.
However, the inclusion of several conservative provisions reduced the likelihood of broad bipartisan support, Politico reported.
The bill includes a series of Republican-backed measures, including a proposal to rename the US Department of Defense as the US Department of War, restrictions on coverage for gender-affirming care and provisions aimed at making it easier for service members to carry personal firearms on military bases.
Republican leaders also added Trump's election-related proposal, the SAVE America Act, to the defence bill following demands from hard-line members who had earlier blocked the legislation, Politico reported.
The traditionally bipartisan defence legislation faced opposition from Democrats, who raised concerns over Trump's handling of the war against Iran, military operations abroad, deployment of National Guard troops to US cities and other administration policies.
A compromise version of the bill is unlikely before the midterm elections, as the House-passed legislation is expected to face challenges in the Senate, where Democrats have already stalled the chamber's own version of the defence bill over concerns related to the Iran war.
Ahead of the vote, US House Armed Services Committee Democrat Adam Smith criticised the Trump administration's defence policies, particularly those of War Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying they had weakened bipartisan support on national security issues.
"We are in an incredibly, incredibly dangerous time. I want to maintain the bipartisan nature of this bill," Smith said, as quoted by Politico.
"But if we're going to do this, we're going to need some Republicans to stand up to the president of the United States and say, 'No'," he added.
Democratic leadership had urged members to oppose the bill, citing disagreements over the defence budget, Iran policy and concerns that Democratic proposals were blocked from receiving votes, Politico reported.
The six Democrats who supported the legislation were Representatives Henry Cuellar of Texas, Don Davis of North Carolina, Jared Golden of Maine, Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, Adam Gray of California and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.
Seven Republican lawmakers opposed the bill, including Josh Brecheen, Tim Burchett, Eli Crane, Harriet Hageman, Anna Paulina Luna, Thomas Massie and Chip Roy.
Despite the partisan divisions, several elements of the legislation received support from both parties.
The bill seeks to accelerate Pentagon acquisition processes to help the military field new technologies more quickly, provides military personnel pay raises ranging from 5 to 7 per cent, and renews restrictions on major troop withdrawals from Europe amid concerns over potential changes to US commitments in NATO countries.
While the NDAA does not directly allocate funds, it is considered a key indicator of congressional support for defence spending. The legislation endorses USD 1.15 trillion in base defence funding requested by the Trump administration through the annual appropriations process.
The remaining portion of Trump's proposed USD 1.5 trillion defence budget, around USD 350 billion, would be addressed through a separate reconciliation bill, Politico reported.
US Congress is also considering a nearly USD 90 billion emergency supplemental request from the White House, including USD 67 billion related to costs associated with the Iran war. Democrats have opposed additional funding for the conflict, while House Republicans are seeking to provide funds through a partisan reconciliation package, Politico reported.
Democrats also secured several provisions in the final bill, including protections for collective bargaining rights of civilian defence employees and a requirement that the Pentagon provide lawmakers with explanations within five days when senior military officers are removed from their positions.

sources.news_title: House GOP Clears Defense Bill by 3 Votes After Floor Drama
sources.text:
Speaker Mike Johnson squeezed a 214-211 procedural vote out of his razor-thin majority Tuesday, advancing a packed slate of Republican priorities, but only after a floor-side huddle with holdouts who nearly sank the whole agenda.
The vote opened debate on four separate legislative tracks at once: a $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, a stock trading ban for members of Congress, a budget framework for a third reconciliation package, and a continuing resolution to keep federal agencies funded at current levels through Dec. 4. A single shift of two votes would have killed the rule and stalled everything.
That outcome looked plausible for much of Tuesday morning. A group of Republican holdouts, enough to block the rule outright, withheld support as the vote clock ran. Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana, and Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota converged on the dissenters in a huddle on the House floor, working them one by one until Reps. Lauren Boebert of Colorado, Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, and Tim Burchett of Tennessee flipped. Only Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky held firm and voted no.
Massie described the holdout bloc's action as a "minor revolt," a phrase that understated the stakes. With Republicans holding one of the slimmest House majorities in modern memory, every procedural vote becomes a potential crisis. Johnson has faced this arithmetic repeatedly, and the pattern is familiar: conservatives leverage the narrow margin to extract concessions, leadership scrambles, and the vote lands with almost no room to spare.
That pattern has produced real consequences before. Earlier this year, GOP rebels sank a procedural vote and forced Johnson to send the chamber home early, an embarrassing breakdown that delayed the legislative calendar for days.
Tuesday's drama followed a similar script but ended differently. The holdouts got their huddle, and most of them got back on board. What they extracted in return was not fully detailed, though one concession was visible in the rule itself: the inclusion of a legislative mechanism known as MIRVing, which merges the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, the SAVE America Act, with the NDAA before the combined package goes to the Senate.
The SAVE America Act requires proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and mandates that voters present identification to cast a ballot. Conservatives have pushed the measure for months, and attaching it to the must-pass defense authorization bill gives it a vehicle that Senate Democrats would find difficult to strip apart. Newsmax reported that Johnson brokered the deal specifically with Luna and conservative holdouts, agreeing to attach the citizenship voting requirement to the NDAA to break the standoff.
The maneuver echoes a tactic Johnson has used before. House conservatives ended a weeks-long blockade on floor votes earlier after Johnson paired a voter ID bill with State Department funding, a pairing that gave the right a reason to vote yes on a package they might otherwise have opposed.
Rep. Virginia Foxx, the North Carolina Republican who chairs the House Rules Committee, framed the defense bill in blunt terms:
"The number one role of the federal government is the defense of this nation."
That argument carried the day. But the three-vote margin showed how fragile the coalition remains.
A minor sideshow played out after the tally. Observers in the gallery reported that Johnson extended his hand to Burchett as the holdouts changed their votes, and that Burchett declined the gesture. Burchett pushed back on the account.
"No, they're in error. I'll shake anybody's hand, I'll shake your hand," Burchett told a reporter, physically shaking the reporter's hand to make the point. He added: "I get angry at him, but I'm not a jerk to him."
The exchange was trivial in substance but revealing in tone. The holdouts were not breaking with leadership on principle so much as pressing for leverage inside a governing majority where every single vote carries outsized weight. Burchett's insistence that he bears no personal animosity toward Johnson underscored the transactional nature of the standoff.
Rep. Victoria Spartz of Indiana presented a different kind of objection. She said she was undecided on the rule because an amendment she sought, one that would have restored terminated pensions for workers at Delphi, the former General Motors auto parts subsidiary, had not been approved for inclusion. Whether Spartz ultimately voted for or against the rule was not reported.
Her complaint pointed to a structural frustration that cuts across the Republican conference. Members with district-specific priorities often find those priorities sidelined when leadership bundles major legislation into omnibus-style procedural packages. The rule that passed Tuesday wrapped four distinct legislative tracks into a single vote, giving individual members little room to separate their support for one measure from their objections to another.
That bundling also included a $95 billion budget reconciliation framework that some Republicans flagged for lacking offsets, meaning the spending would add directly to the deficit without corresponding cuts or revenue elsewhere. The concern was noted but did not produce enough defections to block the rule.
The 214-211 margin is not an anomaly. It is the governing reality for House Republicans. With absences, vacancies, and members willing to break ranks on any given day, Johnson operates with almost no margin for error. Rep. Tom Kean Jr.'s extended absence from Congress has only tightened the math, making every procedural vote a test of whether leadership can hold the line.
The House was expected to take up the stopgap funding measure, the continuing resolution that would keep agencies running through Dec. 4, on Tuesday evening. Final passage of the NDAA could come as early as Wednesday.
Johnson cleared this hurdle. But the fact that a routine procedural vote on a defense bill required a floor-side intervention by the Speaker, the Majority Leader, and the Whip, all three, surrounding a handful of their own members, tells you everything about how narrow the path ahead remains.
Governing with a three-vote margin is not governing with confidence. It is governing on borrowed time, one holdout at a time.

sources.text:
Extension of CISA 2015 info-sharing protections passes as part of House’s defense bill
The House passed an annual defense policy bill on Wednesday that would renew a landmark cybersecurity info-sharing law for another decade.
A provision to extend the 2015 Cybersecurity and Information Sharing Act was included in the chamber’s version of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, which was approved 216-212.
Only a handful of Democrats supported the $1.15 trillion Pentagon policy roadmap that placed no curbs on President Donald Trump's use of U.S. military forces, most notably the Iran war.
The Widespread Information Management for the Welfare of Infrastructure and Government Act would reauthorize CISA 2015, which provides legal protections that allow the private sector and federal government to swap data on criminal and nation-state hacking threats.
The statute briefly expired last year, leaving federal officials in the dark about the full scope of digital threats to U.S. critical infrastructure. It was later temporarily extended through Sept. 30.
The WIMWIG Act was approved by the House Homeland Security Committee last year but has not received a floor vote and faces opposition in the Senate.
Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY), who chairs the Homeland Security Committee, has vowed to block any reauthorization of CISA 2015 unless language is included that would prohibit the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency from engaging in any work to counter online disinformation — even though law and the agency are not directly linked. CISA the agency was created in 2018.
In addition, the Senate’s draft of the NDAA does not include a matching extension, though it is expected to come up on the floor as policymakers work through their amendment process. However, the bill has hit a roadblock with Democrats, who earlier this month tanked consideration of the legislation in their months-long fight to rein in Trump on Iran.
If ultimately included, a renewal would still have to survive negotiations between the two chambers before it could be approved in a final compromise bill.
In May, a group of bipartisan House members also unveiled a legislative proposal on AI that included a similar provision to reauthorize CISA 2015 through 2035, though the package has gained little traction.
Pentagon cyber roles
Another notable difference with the Senate is that the House’s version of the NDAA does not include a provision that would merge the Pentagon’s two major cyber roles into a single leadership post.
The Senate’s draft would create a new “undersecretary of Defense for cyber, information, and networks” to serve as the department’s chief information officer and as the principal cyber adviser to the secretary of Defense.
The provision, which would take effect in two years, is an attempt by lawmakers to get ahead of rising tensions between the CIO and the assistant secretary of defense for cyber policy over who is ultimately responsible for digital operations, especially offensive measures.
The House-passed bill also calls for a “review and realignment” of all Pentagon cyber roles.
Martin Matishak
is the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.
